item.title: Russian warship struck by suspected Ukrainian drones at Libya naval base
item.description:
A Russian warship was struck by a suspected Ukrainian drone at a naval base in Libya's Benghazi, Libyan officials said. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.
They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Satellite imagery appeared to show a boat on fire at the Benghazi port on Sunday, and images captured several hours later appeared to show the same boat partially submerged, CBS partner BBC News reported.
A combination of satellite images shows a Russian corvette and the northern port area before (above) and after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, with the latter image showing the vessel capsized, in Benghazi, Libya, on Nov. 21 and 22, 2026.
Vantor/Handout via REUTERS
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

item.title: Trump says he wants "permanent" deal with Iran
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a "permanent" deal with Iran. On Thursday, he told an Israeli TV network on Thursday that he is "not rushing" and could wait until 2027 to make a decision on his next move in the war with Iran. But sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week that Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, amid the Netanyahu administration's concerns about how rapidly Iran is rebuilding its weapons production capacity.Iran on Thursday rejected Mr. Trump's accusation that it may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons. The foreign ministry said U.S. allegations "keep changing" and are following "the same fraudulent script" as the justification for the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq.
New Updates
11:29 AM
Americans in Bahrain urged to practice "heightened vigilance" amid attacks threat increase
The U.S. Department of State Consular Affairs is urging Americans in Bahrain to practice "heightened vigilance" amid an increase in the threat of attacks by Iran and its allies on U.S. facilities in the region.
"Be aware of potential alerts, flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," the department said in a security alert shared on social media. "Iran has launched attacks targeting U.S. assets in both Kuwait and Bahrain, and Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions."

item.title: U.N. climate summit ends without deal after contentious fossil fuel debate
item.description:
COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.
The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit.
"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."
The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.
Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them.
"We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuel, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU in Antalya. "And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

item.title: Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's wildlife toll
item.description:
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.
In this handout photo provided by the Lewis Pugh Foundation, British endurance swimmer and UNEP Patron of the Oceans Lewis Pugh dives into the Strait of Hormuz, off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.
Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP
Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.
"I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit," he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. "The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now."
Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.

item.title: Violence breaks out in Mexico after capture of drug kingpin wanted by FBI
item.description:
Mexico's military announced Saturday that it had captured a drug kingpin on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted List. Violence broke out in the state of Sinaloa afterwards, rattling civilians.
Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, also known as "El Chapo Isidro," is allegedly the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, which the FBI described as a "heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization" based in Sinaloa.
The cartel is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the U.S., according to the FBI, and has controlled drug production, transportation and distribution throughout Mexico.
Meza-Flores, his second-in-command "Germán" and cartel financial operator "José N" were all taken into custody during a raid in Sinaloa on Friday night, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said on X.
Elite military agents were able to find the targets and then arrive surreptitiously in the area, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. The agents set perimeters around a residence to prevent Meza-Flores from escaping, while also defending the area from reinforcements who could have interrupted the operation.
The arresting agents were attacked with gunfire and explosives, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. Seven attackers were killed during the operation. The agents entered the house and captured Meza-Flores, his two lieutenants, and five other suspected criminals. They also recovered drugs, cash, 10 firearms, a grenade launcher and other ammunition and weapons.
Meza-Flores and his lieutenants were flown to Mexico City and placed in custody of the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime. The other five arrestees were taken into custody in Sinaloa, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. One of those arrested is a first cousin of Meza-Flores and a logistics operator for the cartel.

item.title: Princess Kate reflects on healing in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"
item.description:
Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.
The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.
Catherine, Princess of Wales, meets a cancer patient during a visit to The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust on Sept. 11, 2026, in London, England.
Ian Vogler / WPA Pool / Getty Images
Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.
Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.
